en: The *Navaślokī*:
A Summary of the Meaning of the Noble *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*,
composed by himself in the ocean of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, a mine of auspicious jewels.
All the perfections are established therein through identity with it.
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, non-conceptual, and without abode;
devoid of intrinsic nature, supreme, subtle, and free from *bindu* and *nāda*.
The Perfection of Wisdom is the supreme mother from whom all Buddhas arise;
her nature is the non-apprehension of the three [spheres], and she is the domain of the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
Whoever wishes to correctly cultivate the perfection of wisdom should, in brief, contemplate these nine verses according to their meaning. (Nś 4)
Arising from the power of karma and characterized by the six sense bases,
that which is known as "rebirth" is indeed like a reflection.
Just as one created by magic perceives a magically created city,
so too does one perceive forms— the world created by karma.
Whatever sounds come within the range of hearing from one teaching the Dharma,
all are heard as being like echoes, arising from the faculty of hearing.
That which has been smelled, tasted, and likewise touched by those who crave sense objects—all this that is perceived is like a dream; it does not exist.
Just as a man who is a mechanical puppet performs various actions through illusion,
even so does this body-machine perform actions, though it is devoid of a self.
And those various perceptions that arise at every moment are like mirages; they are seen and then vanish, being devoid of any inherent characteristic.
The object of apprehension is like a reflection, arising from the mind since beginningless time;
and consciousness, possessing that same form, is like a mutual reflection. (NŚ 11)
That which arises from the moon of knowledge within the clear continuum of meditators is indeed like the moon reflected in water; it is not [ultimately] perceptible.
Even the knowledge of yogins has the characteristic of space;
therefore, both knowledge and the object of knowledge are entirely characterized by space.
For one who thus contemplates the reality that is not dependent upon any phenomena,
there will arise the supreme gnosis through the mind of aspiration for enlightenment.
The summary of the meaning of the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom is completed; this work is by the venerable Kambalāmbarapāda.
